## 0. Purpose & scope

A **Workflow** is a project's declaration of which task states exist for it
and which transitions between them are legal. It subsumes the static
`legalTransitions` table (`internal/store/tasks.go`): the workflow becomes the
authority on the task state machine, not a filter layered over one. Today's
table becomes the built-in default workflow every project starts from.

Why: not every project uses every state, and the final state differs by what
the project ships. meetingroom-sync deploys to prod from main and has no
meaningful `deployed_dev`. A data-science project's dataset is effectively
production once it lands from main; `released` is its right terminal, as it is
for CLI tools — while a service with dev and prod environments ends at
`deployed_prod`. Deployment environments are detectable from
`deploy/overlays/`, so the ordinary service case can be inferred rather than
hand-declared.

Settled by WL-69 and taken as given here: definition-of-done is one idea
expressed by two peer objects. **Deliverable** (spec 029, extended by WL-58)
carries the evidence side — what closes a task. **Workflow** (this spec)
carries the state side — which states the project has and how they connect.
Neither owns the other.

Boundary with the rule engine (WL-60): rules choose *which legal edge to take
and when*; the workflow defines *which edges exist*. A rule — LLM-backed or
not — can never add an edge (§6.3).

Out of scope: minting new state names (§1.1 fixes the vocabulary), storing
workflows as spec-025 documents (deliberately left open — storage is a JSON
column, §4), per-repo workflow selection (§7), and workflow-driven cockpit
columns (§5.5).

## 1. The model

### 1.1 Vocabulary and machine are different things

The **state vocabulary** stays global and fixed: `draft`, `ready`,
`in_progress`, `in_review`, `merged`, `deployed_dev`, `deployed_prod`,
`released`, `abandoned` — the nine states of migration `0005_delivery`'s CHECK
constraint and `ns/shapes.ttl`'s `wl:taskState` list. A workflow selects a
subset of this vocabulary and an edge set over it; it never mints a state
name. Every state name that appears anywhere in the system — SQL, wire
shapes, SHACL, UI — is drawn from the vocabulary.

This split is what keeps the subsumption affordable. Code that enumerates
*vocabulary subsets* (delivery ranks, "open" filters, reopenable states)
remains sound in every workflow, because a workflow can only omit states,
never invent them (§5.2). What varies per project is which states a task can
actually occupy and which edges the guard accepts.

### 1.2 The mandatory core

Five states are **mandatory in every workflow**: `draft`, `ready`,
`in_progress`, `merged`, `abandoned`. They are the coordination spine the
backbone itself runs on — claiming, leasing, sweeping, blocking, hierarchy
roll-up, reopen — and making them optional would make cross-project machinery
conditional on project data. A workflow that omits any of them is invalid.

The **core edges** are defined over the whole vocabulary, not just a
workflow's declared states, and are legal in every workflow:

| Core edge | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `draft → ready` | publish |
| `ready → in_progress` | claim / start |
| `in_progress → ready` | release, lease expiry, stop |
| `in_review → in_progress` | rework |
| `ready`·`in_progress`·`in_review` `→ merged` | work landed, or manual `done` |
| `draft`·`ready`·`in_progress`·`in_review` `→ abandoned` | abandon |
| `merged`·`deployed_dev`·`deployed_prod`·`released`·`abandoned` `→ ready` | reopen |

Every core edge targets a mandatory state. The resulting invariant: **a task
can always leave its state along a core edge, whatever its workflow says; a
task can only *enter* an optional state its workflow declares.** This is also
the stranding rule — when a workflow change leaves a task in a state its
workflow no longer declares, the core exits (done, abandon, rework, reopen)
still apply, so no task is ever stuck (§6.4).

### 1.3 Optional states and declared entries

The optional region is the remaining four states, and the only edges a
workflow actually chooses are the **entries into them**:

| Optional state | Legal entry edges |
|---|---|
| `in_review` | `in_progress → in_review` |
| `deployed_dev` | `merged → deployed_dev` |
| `deployed_prod` | `merged → deployed_prod`, `deployed_dev → deployed_prod` |
| `released` | `merged → released`, `deployed_dev → released` |

These source/target pairs are the full set of legal entries — a workflow may
declare a subset of the entries for the optional states it declares, never an
edge outside this table. `deployed_prod → released` remains illegal
everywhere (004 §5.1's deliberate asymmetry), and nothing can ever create
`ready → deployed_prod`: the entry table is a global invariant, not project
data. That is the containment WL-60 relies on — an LLM maintaining a workflow
can vary which delivery tail a project has, and nothing else.

When a workflow declares an optional state and omits `transitions` (§4.1),
all entries from that table among its declared states are implied. Declaring
`in_review` implies its rework and exit edges too — those are core (§1.2).

### 1.4 The default workflow

The built-in workflow named `default` declares all nine states and all
implied entries. Its edge set is, by construction, exactly today's
`legalTransitions` table — the core edges of §1.2 plus every entry of §1.3.
A project that has never touched workflows runs precisely the machine it runs
today; the subsumption changes no behavior until a project opts in.

Workflows carry short descriptive names (lowercase slug, `[a-z0-9-]{1,40}`) —
`service`, `dataset-release`, `prod-from-main` — and an optional
one-sentence `description`. LLMs may propose and maintain them (§6.3); the
name is how a rule, a human, and an audit trail refer to one.

## 2. The guard

> Amends 004 §5.1. The transition table there describes the built-in
> `default` workflow; the authority for any given task is the workflow that
> governs it.

`Transition(tx, now, taskID, from, to, eventID)` keeps its contract — checks
membership of the edge **and** that the task's current state equals `from`,
atomically, appending `state_log` — but membership is now:

```
legal(task, from, to) =
    coreEdge(from, to)                        # §1.2, vocabulary-wide
 ∨  (from, to) ∈ workflowFor(task).entries    # §1.3, declared entries
```

`workflowFor(task)` is resolved inside the same transaction (§3). Wrong
from-state and illegal edge stay `ErrBadTransition`; the error message names
the governing workflow when the edge exists in the vocabulary but not in the
workflow, so "this project has no dev environment" reads as such rather than
as a mystery refusal.

The `tasks.state` CHECK constraint and `ns/shapes.ttl`'s `sh:in` list are
**not** relaxed or made per-project: they enforce the vocabulary (§1.1),
which is still global. Store-level validation enforces workflow membership;
the constraint stays as the vocabulary backstop.

## 3. Which workflow governs a task

Resolution order, evaluated at transition time (not frozen at creation):

1. `tasks.workflow` — a per-task override naming one of the project's
   workflows; set at creation or via `lode task edit --workflow <name>`.
   WL-60's rules become the automated writer of this field later.
2. The project's `default` entry in `projects.workflows` (§4.1).
3. The built-in `default` workflow (§1.4).

Dynamic resolution means editing a workflow immediately applies to every task
governed by it — there is no per-task snapshot to migrate. A `tasks.workflow`
value naming a workflow that no longer exists resolves to the project
default; §4.2 keeps that from happening to open tasks.

Initial states are not workflow business: every task is created `ready`, or
`draft` when the creator says so (`Draft` flag), in every workflow. Both are
mandatory states.

## 4. Storage

A JSON column, deliberately not a spec-025 document: workflows are consulted
inside the transition transaction on the hot path, and coupling the state
machine to the document store was explicitly declined (WL-59). Promoting
workflows to documents later stays open.

### 4.1 Shape

`projects.workflows jsonb NULL`. `NULL` means "built-in default only" — the
column is not backfilled, so existing projects change nothing (§4.3).

```json
{
  "default": "service",
  "workflows": {
    "service": {
      "description": "PR review, then prod straight from main",
      "states": ["draft", "ready", "in_progress", "in_review",
                 "merged", "deployed_prod", "abandoned"]
    },
    "dataset": {
      "description": "datasets are released, not deployed",
      "states": ["draft", "ready", "in_progress", "in_review",
                 "merged", "released", "abandoned"],
      "transitions": [["merged", "released"]]
    }
  }
}
```

- `default` — the name a task with no override resolves to. May name the
  built-in `default`.
- `workflows` — named definitions. A definition is `states` (must include
  the mandatory core) plus optional `transitions`. When `transitions` is
  omitted, every §1.3 entry among the declared states is implied; when
  present, it is the complete list of declared entries (core edges are never
  listed — they are not the workflow's to grant or revoke).

`tasks.workflow text NULL` — the per-task override (§3).

### 4.2 Validation

Enforced in the store on every write of `projects.workflows` and
`tasks.workflow`:

- `states` ⊆ vocabulary; mandatory core ⊆ `states`; no duplicates.
- `transitions` ⊆ the §1.3 entry table, restricted to declared states.
- Every declared optional state has at least one entry edge (implied or
  listed) — an unreachable state is a typo, not a choice.
- `default` names a defined workflow or the built-in `default`.
- Removing or renaming a workflow that open (not closed, per
  `taskClosed`) tasks reference by name is refused, naming the tasks.
  Closed tasks may dangle; they resolve to the project default (§3), and
  their core exits (reopen) remain legal regardless.
- Workflow names match `[a-z0-9-]{1,40}`; `default` is reserved for the
  built-in and cannot be redefined.
- A repo mapping's `done_state` must be a state of the project's default
  workflow; a mismatch is a warning on the write, not a refusal (§7).

A workflow change never moves a task. Tasks sit where they are; the stranding
rule (§1.2) covers states the new definition dropped.

### 4.3 Migration

Migration `0038_project_workflows`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE projects ADD COLUMN workflows jsonb;
ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN workflow text;
```

No backfill, no CHECK changes, no data rewrite. The code migration is the
real work: `legalTransitions` is deleted and replaced by the vocabulary, the
core-edge rules, and the entry table, with the built-in `default` derived
from them; `Transition` resolves the governing workflow in-tx; the direct
table reads in `hierarchy_resolve.go` move to the core rules (§5.4). §5 is
the complete accounting of every reader.

The down migration drops both columns.

## 5. Every state reader, accounted for

The audit behind this section swept `internal/` for state literals,
`legalTransitions` references, and hand-maintained state sets. Each reader
lands in one of four resolutions: **core** (depends only on mandatory states
and core edges — unconditionally correct in every workflow, unchanged),
**vocabulary-static** (enumerates a vocabulary subset as a candidate filter —
stays sound because workflows only omit states; the guard remains
authoritative), **workflow-resolved** (must consult the governing workflow at
runtime), or **display** (degrades gracefully; unknown-to-it states already
render raw).

### 5.1 Core — unchanged, unconditionally correct

| Reader | Dependency |
|---|---|
| `Claim` (`leases.go:201`) | `ready → in_progress`; claimable universe stays literally `state = 'ready'` |
| Lease sweeper / `closeLease` (`leases.go:376`) | rolls back only a task still `in_progress`, via `in_progress → ready`; a task that moved on keeps its state |
| `StartTask` / `StopTask` (`assign.go`) | same two core edges |
| `DeleteTask` parking (`softdelete.go:111`) | `in_progress → ready` |
| Ranking (`ranking.go:69`) | `WHERE t.state = 'ready'` |
| `CreateTask` initial state (`tasks.go:168`) | `draft` / `ready` (§3) |
| `done` endpoint (`lifecycle.go:254`) | `→ merged`; every pre-merged state has a core edge to `merged` |
| `abandon` (`lifecycle.go:262`) | core edges to `abandoned` |
| `reopen` + `reopenableStates` (`lifecycle.go:236`) | the core reopen edges — the set is the vocabulary's post-merged states plus `abandoned`, static because core edges span the vocabulary |
| Hierarchy roll-up (§5.4) | parents move only among core states |
| `patchStateFrom` (`api/tasks.go:424`) | `draft → ready` is core; the `in_progress ↔ in_review` pair stays in the static table and the guard refuses it where the workflow lacks `in_review` — the 422 carries the guard's workflow-naming message (§2) |

### 5.2 Vocabulary-static sets — stay, stay sound

These enumerate vocabulary subsets as prefilters or orderings. A workflow
omitting states only shrinks what they match; none of them grants a
transition, so the guard keeps them honest.

| Reader | Why it stays sound |
|---|---|
| `deliveryRanks` / `deliveredStateSet` / `taskClosed` (`tasks.go:872-952`) | a total order over the vocabulary's delivery tail; ranks of states a workflow omits simply never occur. `taskClosed` — feeding blocking, plan gating, roll-up, doc-lifecycle suppression — is untouched |
| `openWorkExcludedStates` (`participants.go:168`) | derived from `deliveredStateSet` |
| `TasksBelowFrontier` / `PollCandidates` state lists (`delivery_resolve.go:41`, `reconcile.go:81`) | candidate prefilters; the resolver's own transitions go through the guard |
| `mergeCandidateStates` (`hookrun/localmerge.go:16`) | client-side prefilter for the local-merge probe; the server-side resolve is guarded |
| `resolveStatusFilter` open default (`cmd/task.go:415`) | "open" = the vocabulary's pre-delivered states; a workflow lacking `in_review` just never has tasks there |
| `ListTasks` / `?state=` filters | already unvalidated pass-through |
| `validDoneStates` (`projects.go:287`) | unchanged; §7 adds the compatibility warning |
| `tasks_state_check`, `ns/shapes.ttl` `sh:in` | the vocabulary itself (§2) |

`ns/ontology.ttl`'s note that legal transitions "live in internal/store/
tasks.go and are not modelled" (006 Open Q3) becomes "the core rules live in
code; per-project workflows live in `projects.workflows`" — a comment
update, no term change. Projecting workflows into the graph is deferred with
the document-promotion question.

### 5.3 Workflow-resolved — the two real changes

**`ResolveDelivery`** (`delivery_resolve.go`) walks the delivery tail on
observed frontiers. Its pre-merge jump (`ready|in_progress|in_review →
merged`) is core and unchanged. Its tail steps become workflow-resolved: it
advances along the governing workflow's declared entries only — a dev
frontier does nothing for a task whose workflow omits `deployed_dev`
(meetingroom-sync), and the task advances `merged → deployed_prod` directly
when that entry is declared and the prod frontier covers it. The
`done_state = released` branch keeps its meaning through the workflow: a
dataset workflow declares `released` and not `deployed_prod`, so prod
deploys cannot strand it (§7). Container-task early return is unchanged — a
container has no commit, whatever the workflow (§5.4).

**PR-opened hook** (`hooks/github.go:381`): `in_progress → in_review` on
`opened`/`ready_for_review` becomes attempt-and-tolerate — where the
governing workflow declares no `in_review`, the guard refuses and the hook
drops the transition silently, exactly as it already drops any other
non-`in_progress` correlation ("a correlation must never fail the
delivery").

### 5.4 Hierarchy — parents move only in the core

> Amends 004 §6.4, restating it workflow-independently.

The state machine of a task with children is exactly the mandatory core:
`draft → ready` (manual), `ready ↔ in_progress`, `in_progress → merged`,
`in_progress → abandoned`, `merged → ready`. Every roll-up target
(`hierarchy_resolve.go:50-60`) is a mandatory state, so **hierarchy never
consults a workflow** — the roll-up is correct under every workflow by
construction.

`containerForbiddenStates` is redefined from an enumerated set to its actual
meaning: *every non-core state* (`in_review` plus the delivery tail). Those
states are earned by observed facts about a specific commit, and a container
has no commit of its own — the rationale is workflow-independent.
`hierarchy_resolve.go`'s direct reads of `legalTransitions` (`:104-118`)
read the core rules instead; no behavior changes.

### 5.5 Display — degrades gracefully, unchanged in v1

The cockpit's buckets (`cockpit.go:196`, `admin.go:735`) are `in_progress`,
`in_review`, `ready`, and derived `blocked` — two core states, one optional,
one derived. For a workflow without `in_review` the bucket is vacuously
empty; the `t.State == "in_review"` checks stay correct because no task can
enter the state. Workflow-driven columns (a board that shows a project's own
tail) are a cockpit follow-up, not this spec. `StateChip`/`StateLabel`
already fall through to plain rendering for unlisted states. CLI help texts
that spell the vocabulary keep spelling it; the ones that assert legality
(`lode task done`'s stale `in_review -> merged` short) get reworded during
implementation. Obsidian's `state: string` is already untyped.

## 6. Changing a workflow: review, not a gate

### 6.1 Surface

- `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/workflows` — the stored object, or the implied
  built-in default when the column is NULL.
- `PUT /api/v1/projects/{id}/workflows` — full-object replace, validated
  (§4.2), evented (§6.2). Guarded by a `workflow.write` permission granted
  to both `user` and `admin`: the review task is the control, so authorship
  is deliberately not admin-gated — an agent proposing a workflow must not
  need a human in the loop to *write*, only to *review*.
- CLI: `lode project workflow show [--json]`, `lode project workflow set
  --file <json>` (or `-` for stdin), `lode project workflow validate --file`
  (client-side dry run against the same rules). `lode task edit --workflow
  <name>` sets the per-task override.

### 6.2 Event and review task

Every accepted PUT appends a `project.workflows_set` event carrying the full
new object and the actor — provenance for "who changed the machine, when,
to what". A new watcher rule (peer of `doc-lifecycle`, same pure-function
pattern in `internal/watcher`) reacts to it: mint a `review` task in the
project — "Review workflow change on <project>" naming the changed workflow
names — suppressed while an open review task from this rule exists for the
same project. **The change is live from the moment the PUT commits; the
review does not block it.** An admin who rejects the change reverts with
another PUT, which is itself evented — the log holds both moves.

### 6.3 LLM authorship and the WL-60 boundary

LLMs may propose and maintain workflows: discovery (a repo's
`deploy/overlays/`, its environments, whether it releases) suggests which
tail a project needs, and an agent may write it, under §6.2's review. The
containment that made a static `legalTransitions` attractive is preserved by
construction rather than by immutability:

- The mandatory core is not editable at all (§1.2).
- Declared entries are drawn from a fixed table (§1.3); no workflow can
  contain `ready → deployed_prod`, so no prompt-injected rule can take it.
- Rules (WL-60) read workflows and choose among declared edges; they have no
  write path to `projects.workflows`. A rule that wants a new edge is a
  workflow change — evented, reviewed, attributed.

## 7. Relation to `done_state` and Deliverable

`project_repos.done_state` (004 §5.1) keeps its job in v1: the per-repo
marker for "fully delivered", feeding `taskClosed` and the resolver's
frontier logic. Workflow owns *which edges exist*; `done_state` remains the
per-repo pointer at which declared state counts as delivered. The two must
agree — `done_state` must be a state of the governing workflow — and §4.2
makes disagreement a warning. Folding `done_state` into a per-repo workflow
selector (a repo mapping naming a workflow instead of a terminal state) is
the natural next step and is deliberately deferred: it changes repo
discovery and the resolver's per-repo semantics, and nothing above requires
it.

Deliverable (spec 029, WL-58) is untouched: evidence closes a task; the
workflow says which states the task moves through on the way. The two meet
only in prose — a task's definition-of-done is its deliverables *and* its
workflow's delivered states.

## 8. Metrics

Per spec 022's conventions, in the owning packages:

- `worklode_workflow_writes_total{outcome}` — PUT outcomes
  (`ok`/`invalid`/`error`), bounded label values.
- The watcher rule reports through the existing doc-lifecycle rule metric
  with its own rule label (`review-on-workflow-change`).
- Guard refusals stay visible through existing transition error paths; no
  per-state label (unbounded per project) is added.

## 9. Testing

- Store: table tests for the legality rule (§2) — core edges hold in a
  minimal workflow; undeclared entries refuse; stranded states keep their
  core exits; validation rejects each §4.2 violation with a named reason.
- The built-in `default` workflow's edge set is asserted equal to the old
  `legalTransitions` table verbatim — the subsumption proof, kept as a test
  so the equivalence cannot silently drift.
- `TestTaskStateShapeMatchesStateMachine` keeps pinning `ns/shapes.ttl`
  against the vocabulary (now a first-class constant rather than derived
  from the table).
- Resolver: a repo with a `deployed_prod`-only workflow ignores dev
  frontiers; a `released` workflow ignores prod frontiers; both walk their
  declared tail on covered frontiers.
- Watcher: workflows-set event mints one review task, suppressed while one
  is open.
- e2e: one scenario driving a custom-workflow project through the public
  surface — set workflow, PR opened does not enter `in_review` when
  undeclared, prod deploy lands `merged → deployed_prod` directly.

## 10. Non-goals and deferred

- **New state names.** The vocabulary is fixed (§1.1). If a real project
  needs a tenth state, that is a vocabulary change: migration, shapes,
  entry table — a spec amendment, not project data.
- **Workflows as spec-025 documents.** Left open by WL-59; the JSON column
  is the storage until someone decides otherwise.
- **Per-repo workflow selection / retiring `done_state`** (§7).
- **Workflow-driven cockpit columns** (§5.5).
- **Rule-engine semantics** — WL-60's design, bounded by §6.3 here.

## 11. Acceptance criteria

- `legalTransitions` no longer exists; the guard resolves per §2 and the
  built-in default reproduces the old table exactly (test-pinned).
- A project with `workflows` set refuses undeclared entries with an error
  naming the workflow, while every core edge still works.
- A workflow change is evented, mints a non-blocking admin review task, and
  moves no task.
- Existing projects, with the column NULL, behave byte-for-byte as before
  across the e2e suite.
- Every reader in §5 behaves per its stated resolution.
